title: NAU-CSC 111/NAU-SEN: Functions
subject: NAU-CSC111/NAU-SEN 111
description: A prctice CBT exam for NAU-CSC 111/NAU-SEN

questions.question: If f: A → B is an injection and |A| = |B|, then f is necessarily:
questions.explanation: For finite sets, an injection from A to B with equal cardinality is forced to be surjective — hence bijective. Reason: f maps |A| distinct inputs to |A| distinct outputs (injectivity) into a codomain of the same size |B| = |A|, so it uses every codomain element (surjectivity). Option A (constant) contradicts injectivity unless |A| = 1. Option C ("into") means not onto — the opposite of what we just argued. Option D (identity) is too strong: bijective does not imply f(x) = x.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is called 'Surjective' if and only if:
questions.explanation: Surjective (onto) means every element of the codomain B is hit by f — equivalently, the image f(A) equals B. Option B (proper subset) describes a non-surjective function. Option C (|A| < |B|) actually prevents surjectivity, since f can hit at most |A| distinct codomain values. Option D (one-to-one) is injectivity, an independent property — a function can be injective without being surjective (e.g. f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = eˣ).

questions.question: The composition (f ∘ g) is well-defined only if the range of g is a subset of the:
questions.explanation: For (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) to make sense, g(x) must be an element f can accept — i.e. g(x) ∈ domain(f). This requires range(g) ⊆ domain(f). Option A is wrong: composing does not require the output ranges to overlap. Option C (codomain of f) is the target of f, not the input side. Option D is trivially satisfied by g's own definition.

questions.question: An 'Identity Mapping' I_A: A → A is always:
questions.explanation: I_A(x) = x is injective (x₁ ≠ x₂ ⟹ I_A(x₁) ≠ I_A(x₂)) and surjective (every a ∈ A is I_A(a) for a = itself), so it is bijective. Option B (constant) is wrong unless A is a singleton. Option C ("into" = not onto) contradicts surjectivity. Option D is a property of relations, not a classification of functions.

questions.question: If f(x) = 2x+3 is a function from ℝ → ℝ, its inverse f⁻¹(x) is:
questions.explanation: Set y = 2x + 3 and solve for x: y − 3 = 2x, so x = (y − 3)/2. Swap labels to get f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Verify by composition: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2·(x−3)/2 + 3 = (x − 3) + 3 = x. ✓ Option A (2x − 3) does not reverse the operations correctly. Option C (1/(2x+3)) is the reciprocal, not the inverse function — a classic confusion. Option D is unrelated.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is Bijective if and only if its composition with its inverse is:
questions.explanation: For a bijection f, f ∘ f⁻¹ = id_B and f⁻¹ ∘ f = id_A — composing with the inverse returns the identity. This is the operational meaning of "inverse." Option A would collapse everything to one value, which no inverse does. Option C (null) means the composition has no elements, impossible for a bijection. Option D is a definitional mismatch — "surjective-only" is not a type of composition.

questions.question: If the cardinality of set A is greater than set B, a function f: A → B cannot be:
questions.explanation: If |A| > |B|, the pigeonhole principle forces at least two distinct elements of A to share the same image in B — meaning f cannot be injective. (Note: an earlier draft of this explanation had the pigeonhole principle backwards; the correct statement is that more pigeons than holes forces at least two pigeons into one hole.) Option A (surjective) is still possible — surjectivity is constrained by |A| < |B|, not |A| > |B|. Options C and D are both possible.

questions.question: The 'Range' of a function is a subset of the 'Codomain.' Under what condition are they identical?
questions.explanation: Range ⊆ Codomain always; they become equal exactly when the function is onto (surjective) — every codomain element is the image of at least one input. Option A (one-to-one / injective) says distinct inputs produce distinct outputs; this does not force the range to cover the codomain. Option C (reflexive) is a property of relations, not functions. Option D (inclusion) is a specific function type unrelated to surjectivity in general.

questions.question: Given f: A → B and g: B → C, if (g ∘ f) is injective, then:
options: Both f and g must be onto
questions.explanation: Suppose f(a₁) = f(a₂). Then g(f(a₁)) = g(f(a₂)), and since g ∘ f is injective, this forces a₁ = a₂. Therefore f is injective. Notably, g need not be injective on all of B — only on the image f(A). Options C and D are irrelevant: surjectivity is not forced by this hypothesis.

questions.question: Which mapping is defined as f(x) = x for all x ∈ A?
questions.explanation: f(x) = x is the identity mapping — it returns each input unchanged. Option A (inverse) is a different concept, the reverse direction of a bijection. Option C (inclusion) is subtler: it maps a subset into a larger set, embedding it. Option D (constant) sends everything to a single value, the exact opposite.

questions.question: For a function f: A → B, the set B is known as the:
questions.explanation: Codomain is the declared target set B — the set f maps "into." The range is the subset of B actually hit by f. Option A (domain) is the input side A. Option B (range) is the actual outputs, a subset of B. Option D (pre-image) is a related notion: the set of inputs mapping to a specific output.

questions.question: Which type of mapping ensures that no two distinct elements in the domain share the same image?
questions.explanation: Injective (one-to-one) means f(a) = f(b) ⟹ a = b — distinct inputs give distinct outputs. Option A (surjective) guarantees every codomain element is hit but says nothing about domain-side collisions. Option C (bijective) is stronger than needed — bijective = injective + surjective. Option D (constant) is the worst case: every input gives the same output, maximally non-injective.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is Bijective if and only if:
questions.explanation: f is bijective if and only if it has a (unique) inverse f⁻¹: B → A. Surjectivity is needed for f⁻¹ to be defined at every point of B; injectivity is needed for f⁻¹ to give a single well-defined value. Options A and B are each necessary but not sufficient. Option D is the opposite: a constant function is generally neither injective nor surjective.

questions.question: What is the composition (f ∘ g)(x) if f(x) = x² and g(x) = x+1?
questions.explanation: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = f(x + 1) = (x + 1)². Option A (x² + 1) applies f first then adds — that would be (g ∘ f)(x), not (f ∘ g)(x). Option C mixes in extra terms. Option D is linear and cannot arise from squaring. Remember: f ∘ g means "apply g first, then f" — the rightmost function acts first.

questions.question: In an 'Onto' (Surjective) mapping:
questions.explanation: "Onto" is another name for surjective, whose defining property is that the range covers the entire codomain. Option B describes a function that misses part of the codomain (into but not onto). Option C confuses range with domain — different sets in general. Option D only applies to the empty function.

questions.question: A function where every element in the domain has a unique image is:
questions.explanation: "Every element in the domain has a unique image" is injectivity. Note every function already assigns exactly one image to each domain element; injectivity adds that distinct inputs get distinct images. Options A and C are the same concept (surjectivity/onto), about the codomain side. Option D is the extreme opposite.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is surjective if its range is equal to the:
questions.explanation: Surjectivity is precisely range = codomain. The range is what f actually produces; the codomain is B, the set of values f could in principle produce. Making them equal means f "uses up" the whole codomain. Option A confuses the two sides of the arrow. Option C (pre-image) is a related notion but not what defines surjectivity. Option D is unrelated.

questions.question: A function that is both injective and surjective is called:
questions.explanation: Bijective = injective + surjective — a perfect pairing where every domain element maps to a unique codomain element, and every codomain element is hit exactly once. Option A (identity) is one specific bijection, not the general term. Option C ("into") usually means not surjective. Option D refers to a function's inverse, not a classification of the function itself.

questions.question: If f(x) = c for all x in the domain, it is a:
questions.explanation: A function that assigns the same value to every input is a constant function. Option B (identity) does the opposite — each input to itself. Option C (bijective) fails for constant functions unless the domain is a singleton. Option D (linear) usually means f(x) = ax + b with a ≠ 0; a constant is a degenerate case (a = 0), but the standard term for f(x) = c is "constant."

questions.question: Which is required for a function to have an inverse?
questions.explanation: The inverse f⁻¹ exists precisely when f is bijective. Surjective-only (A) leaves ambiguity: a codomain element with two pre-images gives two candidate inverses. Injective-only (B) leaves holes: a codomain element not in the range has no pre-image to invert. Option D is trivially true for all functions and does not distinguish invertible ones.

questions.question: In the function f: A → B, the set of all actual outputs is called the:
questions.explanation: The range (also called the image) is the set of values f actually takes: {f(a) | a ∈ A}. Option A (domain) is the input set A. Option B (codomain) is the target set B, possibly larger than the range if f is not onto. Option D (relation) is the general notion a function is a special case of.

questions.question: A function is injective (one-to-one) if:
options: Every element in the codomain is mapped to
All elements map to the same image
The range is equal to the codomain
questions.explanation: Injectivity says distinct inputs produce distinct outputs: a ≠ b ⟹ f(a) ≠ f(b), equivalently f(a) = f(b) ⟹ a = b. Option A is surjectivity. Option C is the constant function. Option D is another statement of surjectivity (range = codomain). The classic test: "does any output value have two distinct pre-images?" If yes, the function is not injective.

questions.question: A function is surjective (onto) if:
options: Every element in the codomain has at least one pre-image
Every element in the domain maps to exactly one image
questions.explanation: Surjectivity: for every y ∈ B, there exists at least one x ∈ A with f(x) = y — every codomain element is hit. Option B is actually a property of all functions (the functional definition), not specific to surjective ones. Option C is injectivity. Option D is false — bijective functions (which are surjective) do have inverses.

questions.question: For an inverse function f⁻¹ to exist, the function f must be:
questions.explanation: An inverse f⁻¹: B → A must be defined for every element of B (needs surjectivity) and give a single answer (needs injectivity). Together these mean bijective. Option B fails for codomain elements not in the range (no pre-image to invert). Option C fails for codomain elements with two distinct pre-images (which would make f⁻¹ non-functional). Option A is the opposite extreme.

questions.question: If f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, what is the composition (g ∘ f)(x)?
questions.explanation: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(x + 1) = 2(x + 1). Option A (2x + 1) applies +1 after doubling — that would be (f ∘ g)(x), not (g ∘ f)(x). Option C adds 2 instead of doubling. Option D is nonlinear, impossible since both f and g are linear. Remember: g ∘ f means apply f first, then g.

questions.question: What is a function from set A to set B?
options: A rule that assigns exactly one element of B to each element of A
A rule that assigns at least one element of B to each element of A
A rule that assigns exactly one element of A to each element of B
A rule that assigns many elements of B to each element of A
questions.explanation: A function (mapping) from A to B is a rule that assigns exactly one element of B to each element of A. Two requirements: totality (every input gets used) and uniqueness (each input has exactly one output). Option B violates uniqueness ("at least one" allows many). Option C reverses the direction of assignment. Option D violates uniqueness for a single input.

questions.question: In the function notation f: A → B, what does A represent?
questions.explanation: In f: A → B, A is the domain — the set of all possible inputs. Option B (range) is the set of actual outputs, a subset of B. Option A (codomain) is B, the target. Option D (image) is a synonym for range (or sometimes for a specific output f(a)).

questions.question: In the function notation f: A → B, what does B represent?
questions.explanation: B is the codomain — the declared set of possible outputs. Option A (domain) is A, the input set. Option B (range) is the actual outputs, which may be a proper subset of B. Option D (pre-image) is the set of inputs that map to a particular output.

questions.question: What is the range of a function?
options: The set of all possible inputs
The set of all possible outputs
The set of all ordered pairs
questions.explanation: The range is the set of actual outputs — the values f actually produces on its domain. Option A describes the domain. Option B describes the codomain. Option D describes the function itself when represented as a set of ordered pairs, not the range.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition for a binary relation to be a function?
options: Every element in the domain must be related
Each domain element must map to only one codomain element
Every element in the codomain must be mapped to
No element in the domain maps to more than one element in the codomain
questions.explanation: A function requires (i) every domain element to be mapped (option A) and (ii) each domain element to have exactly one image (options B and D restate this). It does not require every codomain element to be hit — that is surjectivity, a stronger property. A function can leave part of the codomain unused and still be a function.

questions.question: Can a one-to-many relation be a function?
options: Yes, if the domain is finite
Yes, if the codomain is infinite
questions.explanation: No, never. A function must map each domain element to exactly one codomain element. A relation that sends a single input to multiple outputs violates the uniqueness requirement and is therefore not a function. Options A, B, and D all try to carve out exceptions that do not exist.

questions.question: Can a many-to-one relation be a function?
options: Yes, it can be a function
questions.explanation: Yes, a many-to-one relation can be a function. A function only forbids one input having multiple outputs; it does not forbid multiple inputs sharing an output. Example: f(x) = x² maps both 2 and −2 to 4 — many-to-one, but a perfectly valid function. Option A confuses many-to-one with one-to-many. Options C and D confuse the question with injectivity/surjectivity, which are additional properties on top of being a function.

questions.question: Given A={1,2,3}, B={a,b,c}, and f={(1,a),(2,b),(3,c)}, is f a function?
options: Yes, it is a valid function
No, because not all elements of B are used
No, because it is not injective
questions.explanation: Yes. Every element of A (1, 2, 3) appears exactly once as a first component, and each maps to exactly one element of B. This satisfies both requirements for a function. Option C confuses "function" with "surjective function" — a function does not need to use every codomain element. Option D confuses "function" with "injective function" — injectivity is not required. Option B is not a valid objection at all.

questions.question: Given R={(1,a),(1,b),(2,c)}, is R a function?
options: No, because 1 maps to two different elements
No, because it is not surjective
questions.explanation: No. The element 1 in the domain appears twice — once paired with a and once with b — so a single input has two different images. This violates the uniqueness requirement. Option C is not a valid objection: 2 mapping to c is fine. Option D confuses "function" with "surjective function." Only the one-to-many violation on input 1 disqualifies R.

questions.question: If f(x) = 2x + 1, what is f(3)?
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 3: f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7. Option A (5) would be 2·2 + 1, substituting x = 2. Option B (6) forgets to add 1. Option D (8) adds 2 instead of 1.

questions.question: Which of the following is a representation of a function as a set of ordered pairs?
options: Arrow diagram with arrows from domain to codomain
Table with x and f(x) columns
questions.explanation: A function can be represented as a set of ordered pairs (a, f(a)). Option B is exactly this: three pairs, each mapping an input to its output. Option A is algebraic-formula representation. Option C is arrow-diagram representation. Option D is tabular representation. All four are valid ways to represent a function; the question asks specifically for the ordered-pairs form.

questions.question: What is an arrow diagram used for in functions?
options: To create a table of values
questions.explanation: An arrow (mapping) diagram shows elements of the domain on one side, elements of the codomain on the other, with arrows from each input to its output. It is a pictorial representation — great for seeing injectivity, surjectivity, and collisions at a glance. Option A describes set-of-pairs form, Option C the algebraic form, Option D the tabular form.

questions.question: Which of the following is an algebraic formula representation of a function?
questions.explanation: An algebraic formula expresses the function as an equation relating input to output, e.g. f(x) = x² + 1. Option A is the ordered-pairs form. Option B is the arrow-diagram form. Option D is the tabular form. Each of the four representations is a legitimate way to describe the same function.

questions.question: In a table representation of a function, what is typically shown?
options: Pairs of x and f(x) values
questions.explanation: A table representation shows pairs — one column of inputs x and one column of corresponding outputs f(x). Option A and B list only one side of the pair. Option D is a different concept entirely: the inverse is a function, not a column in a table of f.

questions.question: What is the domain of a function?
options: The set of all possible outputs
The set of all possible inputs
The set of all ordered pairs
questions.explanation: The domain is the set of all possible inputs — the values x for which f(x) is defined. Option A describes the codomain (possible outputs). Option C describes the range (actual outputs). Option D describes the function itself when written as a set of pairs.

questions.question: What is the codomain of a function?
options: The set of all possible inputs
The set of all possible outputs
The set of all ordered pairs
questions.explanation: The codomain is the declared target set — the set of possible outputs. Option A is the domain. Option C is the range (the actual outputs), which may be a proper subset of the codomain if the function is not onto. Option D is the function itself.

questions.question: Which type of function maps two or more domain elements to the same codomain element?
questions.explanation: A many-to-one function sends two or more inputs to the same output — e.g. f(x) = x² maps 2 and −2 both to 4. Option A (one-to-one / injective) forbids this by definition. Option C (onto / surjective) is about covering the codomain, not about domain-side collisions. Option D (into) is about not covering the codomain. Note many-to-one functions are perfectly valid functions; they are just not injective.

questions.question: Which type of function does not map to every element in the codomain?
questions.explanation: An into function (also called "not onto") leaves at least one codomain element without a pre-image — its range is a proper subset of its codomain. Option A (surjective) is the opposite: it hits every codomain element. Option B (injective) says nothing about covering the codomain. Option D (bijective) is both injective and surjective, so it covers the codomain completely.

questions.question: What is a constant function?
options: A function where each element maps to itself in the codomain
A function where all elements map to the same image
A function that is both injective and surjective
A function or mapping that has no inverse
questions.explanation: A constant function maps every element of the domain to the same single element of the codomain — e.g. f(x) = 5 for all x. Option A describes the identity function. Option C describes a bijection. Option D is unrelated to constancy (in fact some constant functions with singleton domains do have inverses).

questions.question: What is an identity function?
options: A function where each element maps to itself
A function where all elements map to the same element
A function that is not injective
A function that is not surjective
questions.explanation: An identity function maps each element to itself: f(x) = x for all x in the domain. Option B describes the constant function (opposite extreme). Options C and D are false: the identity function is in fact both injective and surjective (hence bijective).

questions.question: Which of the following is a property of a bijective function?
questions.explanation: A bijective function is both one-to-one (injective) and onto (surjective), so it has a well-defined inverse function f⁻¹. Options A and B describe only one half of bijectivity. Option D is the opposite — a constant function is generally neither injective nor surjective (unless the domain is a singleton).

questions.question: What is a one-to-one correspondence?
options: A function that is injective but not surjective
A function that is surjective but not injective
A function that is both injective and surjective
questions.explanation: A one-to-one correspondence is another name for a bijection — a function that is both injective and surjective, pairing every element of the domain with exactly one element of the codomain and vice versa. Options A and B describe half-bijections. Option D is the extreme opposite.

questions.question: When does a function f: A → B have an inverse?
options: If and only if f is injective
If and only if f is surjective
If and only if f is bijective
questions.explanation: A function has an inverse if and only if it is bijective. Injectivity is needed so f⁻¹ is well-defined (single value per output); surjectivity is needed so f⁻¹ is defined on the whole codomain. Option A is false — most functions have no inverse. Options B and C each capture only one of the two required conditions.

questions.question: If f: A → B and g: B → C, what is the composition g ∘ f?
options: A function from A to C defined by (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))
A function from B to B
A function from C to A
A function from A to B
questions.explanation: g ∘ f: A → C, defined by (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Apply f first (A → B), then g (B → C), so the composite goes A → C. Option B (B → B) is wrong unless A = C = B, which is not required. Option C reverses the direction. Option D stops at B, but the composite goes all the way to C.

questions.question: Which of the following is an importance of functions in computer science?
questions.explanation: Functions are central to computer science because they model program input-output behavior (every subroutine is a function), underpin mathematical modeling (physics engines, graphics, simulations), are the backbone of algorithms and recursion (recursive functions define themselves in terms of smaller versions of themselves), and additionally support database mappings (query functions) and machine-learning/AI models (activation functions, loss functions). All three listed options are correct.
